detailed_rationale:
Jindal Steel's Angul expansion from 6 to 12 MTPA is a completed fact, not a slide-deck promise: BOF-2, BOF-3 (3 MTPA) and a 4.6 MTPA blast furnace ("Bhagavati Subhadrika") were all commissioned during FY26, and the company announced completion in March 2026, taking total crude-steel capacity to 15.6 MTPA (12 Angul + 3.6 Raigarh) from 9.6 MTPA. FY26 delivered record production of 9.25 MT (+14% YoY) and sales of 8.68 MT (+9% YoY), and management is guiding FY27 production of 11.0-11.5 MT and sales of 10.5-11.0 MT (+21-27% YoY) — still only ~70-75% utilization of the new nameplate, so genuine multi-year volume runway exists without further capex. CEO Gautam Malhotra's own framing on the Q4 FY26 call was that the company is "focusing on achieving capacity utilization first, followed by mix optimization," with movement expected in H1 FY27 and stabilization only by year-end — a phased ramp, not a light switch.

The financial reality check is the crux of this call: despite record volumes, EBITDA per tonne FELL from ₹11,712 in FY25 to ₹10,482 in FY26, as rising coking-coal costs ate the benefit of price recovery — the operating leverage the market is pricing in has not shown up yet. Q4 FY26 consolidated PAT of ₹1,041-1,044cr reversed a ₹339cr Q4 FY25 loss, but FY26 itself carried a further ₹1,433cr impairment flagged on Australian assets (per the earnings call), on top of the ~₹1,229.5cr Wollongong Resources/Madagascar impairment already taken around Q4 FY25 — a recurring, not one-off, drag from a stranded non-core overseas coal asset. FY26 consolidated PAT was ₹3,361cr against a market cap of roughly ₹1.05 lakh crore, i.e. an ROE of only ~7-8% (consistent with this desk's own quant read of 0.07), yet the stock trades near 31x trailing consolidated earnings (some trackers show ~26x on a freshly rebased TTM base post the strong Q4 print) and ~2x book value (book value ~₹499/share vs CMP ~₹1,025). Balance-sheet discipline is real and improving — consolidated net debt ₹16,019cr as of March 2026, net debt/EBITDA down to 1.66x from 1.72x, and CARE upgraded the long-term rating to AA+/Stable (from AA/Stable) on July 1, 2026 for both the parent and subsidiary Jindal Steel Odisha Ltd (JSOL), citing the completed expansion and satisfactory utilization; management guides net debt/EBITDA below 1.5x by Q2 FY27, helped by a slurry pipeline going live in Q1 FY27 (₹750-1,000/tonne cost saving once ramped) and captive raw-material progress (Utkal B1/C, Gare Palma IV/6 coal blocks operationalized). Iron ore was ~92% captive in FY26, but management itself flagged this will fall to 40-50% once the next capacity leg ramps, since overall ore demand will outpace captive mine growth.

Policy is a genuine tailwind: the 12% safeguard duty on steel imports was extended for three years in December 2025 (a hike to 24% is reportedly under government consideration), and a fresh anti-dumping investigation into hot-rolled coil from China/Japan/Russia was launched June 25, 2026 — both reduce import-led spread-compression risk. But the next leg of the growth story — scaling Angul to 25.2 MTPA by 2030 via JSOL, on a reported ₹47,043cr total program with only ₹9,574cr invested so far — is a considerably bigger execution bet than the one just finished, and that first leg alone took roughly seven years from announcement to completion. Governance is unremarkable: promoter holding is high and rising (62.7%), a minor pledge (1.7mn shares, 0.17% of capital) was released in June 2026 on the O.P. Jindal-family side (not Naveen Jindal's core holding), and no fresh red flags surfaced. Q1 FY27 results are scheduled for board approval on July 24, 2026 and are not yet out — the first live read on whether the ramp is tracking guidance.
recommendation_rationale: Sell, not Hold, because the valuation (~31x trailing earnings, ~7-8% ROE) is pricing in a smooth, SIMULTANEOUS volume ramp and spread recovery that FY26's own numbers do not yet show — EBITDA per tonne went DOWN, not up, in the very year capacity was completed and volumes hit a record. That is the opposite of what a rich multiple should require. Layer on a recurring (not one-time) overseas impairment problem and a much larger, still-unexecuted next capacity leg (25.2 MTPA by 2030) following a first leg that itself ran roughly seven years, and the balance of risk sits with disappointment, not surprise. This aligns with the desk's own quant score (Reduce 3y / Avoid 1y, quality score 45, growth_3y_score under 10). The credit-rating upgrade and safeguard-duty tailwind are real, but they support "the balance sheet won't blow up," not "today's multiple is earned."
summary: Jindal Steel has genuinely completed a large capacity expansion — its Angul plant doubled to 12 million tonnes a year in March 2026, taking total capacity to 15.6 million tonnes — and management is guiding 21-27% volume growth for FY27 off capacity that already exists. That part is real. But profit per tonne of steel actually fell last year even as volumes hit a record, because raw-material costs rose faster than steel prices recovered, and the stock trades at roughly 31 times last year's earnings against a return on equity of only about 7-8%. The balance sheet is in better shape — credit rating just upgraded, debt levels improving — and government import duties support domestic steel prices. But the share price already assumes the expanded capacity will ramp up smoothly and margins will recover meaningfully — two things that have not happened together yet, and this company's own history shows expansions taking years longer than first announced. We rate it Sell on valuation grounds, not on the underlying growth story.
positive_para: The bull case is evidence-backed, not aspirational. The Angul 6-to-12 MTPA expansion is DONE — commissioned in March 2026 with BOF-2, BOF-3 and a 4.6 MTPA blast furnace all operational — taking total company capacity to 15.6 MTPA from 9.6 MTPA, and FY26 already delivered record production (9.25 MT, +14% YoY) and sales (8.68 MT, +9% YoY) even before the new capacity was fully absorbed. FY27 guidance of 11.0-11.5 MT production / 10.5-11.0 MT sales (+21-27%) is achievable off capacity that physically exists, not capex still to be spent. Balance-sheet discipline is real: net debt/EBITDA improved to 1.66x (from 1.72x) as of March 2026, CARE upgraded the long-term rating to AA+/Stable on July 1, 2026 for both the parent and the JSOL subsidiary, and management guides leverage below 1.5x by Q2 FY27. Near-term margin levers are concrete and dated: the iron-ore slurry pipeline goes live in Q1 FY27 for an estimated ₹750-1,000/tonne cost saving, and captive coal blocks (Utkal B1, Utkal C, Gare Palma IV/6) are ramping. Policy is a tailwind: the 12% safeguard duty on steel imports was extended for three years in December 2025 (a hike to 24% is under consideration), plus a fresh anti-dumping probe into Chinese/Japanese/Russian HRC imports launched in June 2026 — both cut the risk of import-led spread compression just as the new capacity comes online. Sell-side sentiment has also turned more constructive, with fresh coverage initiations and rising consensus expectations.
negative_para: The strongest bear point is that the operating leverage the market is paying for has not shown up: EBITDA per tonne fell from ₹11,712 in FY25 to ₹10,482 in FY26, in the very year record volumes were delivered, because rising coking-coal costs ate the benefit of price recovery. That is the opposite of what a ~31x trailing multiple (ROE just ~7-8%, matching this desk's own quant read) should require — expanding capacity should be improving unit economics, and for FY26 it did not. Layered on top, Jindal Steel keeps taking impairments on a non-core, stranded Australian coal asset (Wollongong Resources) — roughly ₹1,229.5cr around Q4 FY25 and a further ₹1,433cr flagged in Q4 FY26 — a recurring, not one-time, drag that raises capital-allocation questions outside the core steel business. Iron-ore self-sufficiency, by management's own admission, is set to FALL from ~92% captive in FY26 to 40-50% once the next capacity leg ramps, because ore demand will simply outpace captive mine growth — a genuine raw-material cost exposure the market is not obviously pricing. And the next leg of the growth story — scaling Angul to 25.2 MTPA by 2030 through JSOL, on a reported ₹47,043cr total program with only ₹9,574cr spent so far — is a much bigger execution bet than the one just completed, and that first leg alone took roughly seven years from announcement to completion. A name with unresolved execution risk, a margin trend running the wrong way, and a recurring overseas impairment problem does not, in our judgment, clear a 31x multiple.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At ~31x trailing consolidated EPS (some trackers show ~26x on a freshly rebased TTM number post the strong Q4 print) and roughly 2x book value, the market is underwriting a full, simultaneous volume-ramp-plus-spread-recovery scenario. FY26 consolidated PAT was ₹3,361cr against a ~₹1.05 lakh crore market cap; to bring the multiple down to a more normal through-cycle steel multiple of ~12-15x without any further re-rating, normalized PAT would need to roughly double-to-triple from the FY26 base — plausible only if volumes ramp from 8.68 MT toward the 15.6 MTPA nameplate (FY27 guidance of 10.5-11.0 MT sales gets partway there) AND EBITDA/tonne recovers well above the FY26 print of ₹10,482 (which itself fell YoY) toward the ₹15,000-17,000/tonne levels some sell-side models now assume for FY27-28 on slurry-pipeline savings and captive-coal ramp. That is a plausible multi-year path, but it requires both legs to work at once, with limited room for the kind of commissioning slippage (seven years for the first 6 MTPA leg) or coking-coal cost shocks that already showed up once in FY26. Verdict: rich-to-fair, not cheap — the price already spends the ramp's upside before it has been delivered.
